newsitem.title: THAILAND: Thai livestock growth seen driving up feed demand.
newsitem.headline: Thai livestock growth seen driving up feed demand.

text.p: Growth in the Thai livestock industry over the next five years could drive up demand for animal feeds to some 13 million tonnes a year by 2001 from 10 million now, a feedmill industry leader said on Thursday.
Prasit Damrongchietanon, president of the Thai Feed Mill Association, told Reuters the livestock industry was projected to grow by five to seven percent between 1997-2001.
"The growth will be driven by a rise in both local consumption and exports. The figure is based on the assumption that we will also export pork in the future," he said.
Thais comsumed an average of 12 kg (26.4 lb) of chicken meat per year and the quantity was set to rise, he said.

Thailand is the biggest exporter of frozen chicken meat in Southeast Asia, but barely exports pork. It is also the world's fifth largest frozen poultry exporter after the United States, the European Union, Brazil and China.
It exported 160,000 tonnes of frozen chicken meat in 1996, when global consumption was estimated at 32.7 million tonnes.

Prasit, also a senior executive at agri-business conglomerate Charoen Pokphand, projected demand for major animal feed ingredients such as soymeal would surge to 2.5 million tonnes by 2001 from 1.6-1.8 million tonnes this year.
Demand for corn will rise to six million tonnes by that time against approximately four million at present, he added.
"Of the total increased demand, 70-80 percent will be imported," he said.
Prasit urged the government to fully liberalise imports of feed ingredients. He said the association recently asked the commerce ministry to consider removing soymeal tariffs.
The Thai government has for some time strictly regulated imports of animal feed raw materials to protect local farmers.

But since this year it has relaxed the rules somewhat. The government removed the import quota on soybean and soymeal and also lifted import tariffs for soybean. The government also cut the tariff for soymeal to 10 percent from 15 percent.

However, to protect local farmers, corn imports remain controlled by the government, which recently allowed zero-tariff corn imports of 200,000 tonnes on the condition average prices of domestic grain during certain periods must not be lower than 4.50 baht ($0.17) per kg.
He said the government should help farmers by providing subsidies while at the same time freeing up imports.

"The current system makes it difficult for the industry to manage the cost of production and supplies effectively...This affects the price stability of foods and consequently the consumers," Prasit said.

"The word subsidy might not be popular...but name me one major country that does not help its farmers this way. Thailand cannot afford to ignore its farmers...But the government should not protect them the way it is doing now as the burden is passed on to other sectors," he said.
